name: Citation Graphs Over Time
title: Citation Graphs Over Time
answer: Citation graphs over time are the record of which research works cite which others, arranged so that the order of publication and the direction of influence are both visible. The unit is the paper and the edge is a citation, and the interesting object is how that structure changes as new work arrives. A static citation graph answers who cites whom, while a temporal one answers when a link appeared, which papers gained attention after a delay, and which lines of work went quiet. This matters for literature review, for tracing the origin of an idea, and for judging whether a claim rests on a single thread or on many independent ones.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is bibliographic metadata: titles, authors, venues, years, and reference lists, usually pulled from services such as Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, or PubMed. Storage is typically a graph database or a columnar store, because citation edges are numerous and queries often walk several hops. Snapshotting matters, since a graph rebuilt today will not match one built last year, and versioned snapshots let a study compare the two.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work begins with entity resolution, matching author names and paper records that differ across sources, then with parsing reference strings into clean edges. From there the common operations are traversal, such as finding all works that cite a given paper, and ranking, such as counting citations within a window or weighting by venue. Temporal analysis adds time slices, so the graph can be cut at a year and compared with the slice before it, which exposes bursts, decay, and the lag between publication and recognition. Community detection and path finding are used to group related work and to trace how one result reached another, and the outputs are usually read as maps rather than as verdicts on quality.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Citation data carries attribution obligations, and reuse terms differ between sources, so a project needs to know what each provider permits and how to credit it. Author disambiguation is a known source of error, and a misattributed paper can follow a researcher for years, so corrections need a route back into the record. Citation counts are also easy to misread as measures of merit when they mostly measure visibility and age, and self citation and citation cartels distort them further. Any derived claim should point to the original paper, which is the practice followed here, and the graph should be treated as a finding aid rather than as evidence about a person.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward graphs that update continuously rather than in annual dumps, with provenance attached to each edge so a reader can see where a link came from. Full text linking, rather than reference string matching, would let a graph distinguish a paper cited for its method from one cited for its data. Better handling of preprints and of non English venues would reduce the bias toward well indexed English language journals. The open question is whether richer graphs improve discovery or simply make existing attention patterns more efficient to reproduce.
